items.title: The content of a node and the content vector of a standard tableau
items.statement: Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), so that the nodes of $[\lambda]$ are the pairs $(r,c)$ with $r,c\ge1$ and $c\le\lambda_r$ (rows numbered downward, columns rightward). The **content** of a node $(r,c)\in[\lambda]$ is $$c(r,c):=c-r,$$ the column index minus the row index. The node $(r,c)$ therefore has content $t$ exactly when it lies on the diagonal $c-r=t$; the content of $(1,1)$ is $0$, contents increase by $1$ along a row and decrease by $1$ down a column. Now let $T$ be a standard tableau of shape $\lambda$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). For $1\le k\le n$ let $(r_k,c_k)$ be the node of $[\lambda]$ carrying the entry $k$, so that $T(r_k,c_k)=k$. The **content vector** of $T$ is $$\operatorname{Cont}(T):=\bigl(c_T(1),\dots,c_T(n)\bigr)\in\mathbb Z^n,\qquad c_T(k):=c(r_k,c_k)=c_k-r_k,$$ the list of contents of the nodes read in the order of the entries $1,2,\dots,n$. For the empty tableau of shape $\varnothing$ the content vector is the empty vector, the unique element of $\mathbb Z^0$.
items.strategy: Read the contents in entry order; the node coordinates are the English row/column coordinates of the published partition item, so rows increase downward and the content of $(r,c)$ is $c-r$. The map $T\mapsto\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ depends only on the positions of the entries, and the content vector of a tableau of shape $\lambda$ has multiset of entries equal to the multiset of contents of the nodes of $[\lambda]$.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, section 5, printed pp. 17-22
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), section 3, printed pp. 18-25

items.title: The Gelfand-Tsetlin algebra of the symmetric group chain
items.statement: For $n\ge1$ and $1\le m\le n$ let $Z(\mathbb C[S_m])$ be the centre of the complex group algebra $\mathbb C[S_m]$ ([[def-center-of-the-group-algebra]], [[def-group-ring]]). We use the standard chain of symmetric groups $$S_1\subset S_2\subset\cdots\subset S_n,\qquad S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\}),$$ in which $S_m$ is the subgroup of $S_n$ fixing every element of $\{m+1,\dots,n\}$ pointwise; thus $\mathbb C[S_m]$ is the subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$ spanned by $S_m$, and $Z(\mathbb C[S_1])=\mathbb C\cdot1$. Each centre $Z(\mathbb C[S_m])$ is thereby regarded as a subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$. The **Gelfand-Tsetlin algebra** of the chain is $$\mathrm{GZ}(n):=\bigl\langle Z(\mathbb C[S_1]),Z(\mathbb C[S_2]),\dots, Z(\mathbb C[S_n])\bigr\rangle\subseteq\mathbb C[S_n],$$ the unital subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$ generated by all these centres.
items.strategy: The centre of each $\mathbb C[S_m]$ is a subalgebra of the semisimple algebra $\mathbb C[S_m]$, and the chain inclusions identify it with a subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$; the generated algebra is commutative because each centre is generated by the class sums of $S_m$, and class sums of $S_m$ and $S_k$ centralize one another in $\mathbb C[S_{\max(m,k)}]$.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 1-2, printed pp. 7-12

items.title: The Jucys-Murphy elements of the symmetric group algebra
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$ and let $R$ be a commutative ring. In the group ring $R[S_n]$ of the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]], [[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-group-ring]]), where $(j\ k)$ denotes the transposition of the distinct entries $j,k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **Jucys-Murphy elements** are $$X_1:=0,\qquad X_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(j\ k)\in R[S_n]\qquad(2\le k\le n).$$ Each $X_k$ is a finite sum of group elements with coefficient $1$, so the formula already defines an element of the integral group ring $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, and its image under the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to R[S_n]$ is the displayed element ([[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]); for $1\le k\le m\le n$ the element $X_k$ of $R[S_m]$, computed in the subgroup $S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\})\subseteq S_n$ of permutations fixing $m+1,\dots,n$, maps to $X_k$ under the inclusion $S_m\hookrightarrow S_n$. Equivalently $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$, where $T_k=\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}(i\ j)$ is the sum of all transpositions in $S_k$.
items.strategy: Use finite integral sums, the domain 1<=k<=m<=n, subgroup inclusions and the base-change homomorphism. Separate transpositions by their largest letter to prove X_k=T_k-T_(k-1).

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, section 3, printed pp. 12-15
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), section 3, printed pp. 18-25

items.title: Every element of $S_n$ is inverted by an involution of $S_{n-1}$
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$, let $S_{n-1}\le S_n$ be the stabilizer of $n$, and let $g\in S_n$. There is $h\in S_{n-1}$ with $h^2=1$ (the identity is allowed) and $hgh^{-1}=g^{-1}$; here such a self-inverse permutation is called an involution. In particular every element of $S_n$ is conjugate to its inverse by an element of $S_{n-1}$.
items.strategy: Reverse each disjoint cycle explicitly, fixing n in its own cycle, to construct h with h^2=1 and hgh^-1=g^-1. The identity is allowed for n=1,2. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, Lemma 2.2, printed p. 9; its deletion argument is replaced by the explicit cycle-reversal proof below
K. Conrad, Conjugacy Classes (cycle conjugation), as cited by the published cycle-conjugation lemma

items.title: The Jucys-Murphy elements commute pairwise
items.statement: For all $1\le i,j\le n$ one has $X_iX_j=X_jX_i$ in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, hence in $R[S_n]$ for every commutative ring $R$; that is, the Jucys-Murphy elements commute pairwise, and the subalgebra they generate is commutative.
items.strategy: Induct on $n$. The transposition sum $C_2^{(n)}=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(i\ j)=\sum_{k=2}^nX_k$ is central in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, because conjugation permutes the transpositions of $S_n$. Assume $X_2,\dots,X_{n-1}$ commute; as elements of $S_n$ they satisfy $\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}X_k=C_2^{(n)}-X_n$, and comparing $X_j C_2^{(n)}=C_2^{(n)}X_j$ with $X_j\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}X_k=\big(\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}X_k\big)X_j$ gives $X_jX_n=X_nX_j$ for $2\le j\le n-1$; combined with the induction hypothesis this covers all pairs. The argument is integral and uses no choice.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), section 3, printed pp. 18-25, Theorem 3.1(a)

Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, equation (2.1) and its following commutativity observation, printed p. 10

items.title: A partition is determined by the multiset of its node contents
items.statement: Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$. If the multiset of contents $\{c(x):x\in[\lambda]\}$ equals the multiset $\{c(y):y\in[\mu]\}$, then $\lambda=\mu$.
items.strategy:
For a partition $
u$ and an integer $t$ let $n_t(
u):=\#\{x\in[
u]:c(x)=t\}$. The node $(i,j)$ has content $j-i$, so for $t\ge0$, $n_t(
u)=\#\{i:
u_i-i\ge t\}$, and for $t<0$, $n_t(
u)=\#\{j:
u'_j-j\ge -t\}$; the counts on nonnegative diagonals therefore determine the multiset of diagonal differences $
u_i-i$ over the diagonal nodes $i\le
u_i$, and those are the Frobenius arm lengths $a_i=
u_i-i$, while the counts on negative diagonals determine the leg lengths $b_j=
u'_j-j$. Since $[
u]$ is recovered from its Frobenius coordinates $(a_i),(b_i)$ by $
u_i=\#\{j:a_j\ge i\}+\#\{j:b_j\ge i\}$ (equivalently, the diagram is the union of the arm and leg hooks along the main diagonal), equal content multisets force equal Frobenius data and hence $\lambda=\mu$. The same recovery is what makes the central interpolation of the next theorem well posed.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), sections 3-5, printed pp. 18-45 and Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 51-52

Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal Forms and Gram Determinants for Cellular Algebras, J. reine angew. Math. 619 (2008) 141-173; arXiv:math/0604108, sections 2.8-2.15, 3.1-3.7, Theorem 3.16, Corollary 3.17 and Proposition 4.13, printed pp. 4-21

items.title: Distinct addable nodes of a partition have distinct contents
items.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a partition. If $x\ne y$ are addable nodes of $[\lambda]$, then $c(x)\ne c(y)$; equivalently the content map is injective on the set $\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ of addable nodes.
items.strategy: An addable node is the last node $(r,\lambda_r+1)$ of a row $r$ with $\lambda_{r-1}>\lambda_r$ (with $\lambda_0=\infty$), and its content is $\lambda_r+1-r$. If $r<r'$ are two such rows, then $\lambda_r\ge\lambda_{r'}$ because $\lambda$ is a partition, so $\lambda_r+1-r>\lambda_{r'}+1-r'$; the two contents differ. This nonvanishing is what makes all denominators in the interpolation projectors of the next items nonzero.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), sections 3-5, printed pp. 18-45 and Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 51-52
Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 1-7, printed pp. 7-25

items.title: Local relations between the Jucys-Murphy elements and adjacent transpositions
items.statement: Let $n\ge2$ and put $s_i:=(i\ i+1)$ for $1\le i\le n-1$, the Coxeter generators of $S_n$. Then in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, hence in $R[S_n]$ for every commutative ring $R$: (a) $s_iX_j=X_js_i$ whenever $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; (b) $s_iX_i+1=X_{i+1}s_i$; equivalently $s_iX_is_i+s_i=X_{i+1}$ and $s_iX_{i+1}=X_is_i+1$. In particular the subalgebra generated by $s_i,X_i,X_{i+1}$ satisfies the local $H(2)$ relations $s_i^2=1$, $X_iX_{i+1}=X_{i+1}X_i$, $s_iX_i+1=X_{i+1}s_i$.
items.strategy: Conjugation fixes or permutes summands outside the adjacent pair. Compute s_i X_i = X_(i+1) s_i - 1; multiply by s_i for the equivalent forms. Subgroup-central transposition sums give adjacent commutation. The finite generated algebra satisfies H(2) relations; no dimension or universal presentation is asserted.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), section 3, printed pp. 18-25, Theorem 3.1
Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, section 3, printed pp. 12-15
Michael Muger, Tensor Categories: A Selective Guided Tour, section 4 (Coxeter presentation of the symmetric group)

items.title: The centralizer of $\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]$ in $\mathbb C[S_n]$ is commutative
items.statement: Let $$Z(\mathbb C[S_n],\mathbb C[S_{n-1}])=\{z\in\mathbb C[S_n]: zh=hz\text{ for every }h\in S_{n-1}\}$$ be the centralizer of the subalgebra $\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]$ in $\mathbb C[S_n]$. Then $Z(\mathbb C[S_n],\mathbb C[S_{n-1}])$ is a commutative subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$.
items.strategy: Let $\sigma$ be the linear anti-automorphism of $\mathbb C[S_n]$ with $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$ for group elements. For $z=\sum_g c_gg$ in the centralizer and any $g\in S_n$, choose by the previous item an involution $h\in S_{n-1}$ with $hgh^{-1}=g^{-1}$; since $z$ commutes with $S_{n-1}$ we have $z=hzh^{-1}=\sum_g c_g\,hgh^{-1}=\sum_gc_gg^{-1}=\sigma(z)$ when both sides are expanded in the basis $S_n{}$ and coefficients are compared, because $g\mapsto hgh^{-1}$ permutes the group basis. Hence $\sigma$ is the identity on the centralizer, and for $y,z$ in the centralizer $yz=\sigma(yz)=\sigma(z)\sigma(y)=zy$. The argument uses the group basis and the inversion anti-automorphism only; it is choice-free and independent of Maschke's theorem.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, Theorem 2.1 and its complete coefficient-inversion proof, printed pp. 9-10

items.title: Elementary symmetric Jucys-Murphy evaluations are cycle-count class sums
items.statement: For $n\ge1$ and $0\le s\le n$, $$e_s(X_2,X_3,\dots,X_n)=\sum_{\substack{\rho\vdash n\\ \ell(\rho)=n-s}}C^{(n)}_\rho,$$ where the right-hand side is the sum of all permutations of $S_n$ with exactly $n-s$ cycles (fixed points counted), grouped into conjugacy classes; it is zero for $s>n-1$. In particular $e_0=1$, $e_1$ is the sum of all transpositions, and $e_{n-1}$ is the sum of all $n$-cycles.
items.strategy: Induct on $n$ using $X_k^{(n)}=X_k^{(n-1)}$ for $k\le n-1$ and the elementary-symmetric recursion $$e_s(X_2^{(n)},\dots,X_n^{(n)})=e_s(X_2^{(n-1)},\dots,X_{n-1}^{(n-1)})+X_ne_{s-1}(X_2^{(n-1)},\dots,X_{n-1}^{(n-1)}).$$ By induction the first term is the sum of all permutations of $S_{n-1}$ with $n-s-1$ cycles (correcting for the fixed point $n$: as elements of $S_n$ these have $n-s$ cycles and fix $n$), and the second term is $\sum_\sigma X_n\sigma=\sum_{\sigma, j}(j\ n)\sigma$ over permutations $\sigma$ of $S_{n-1}$ with $n-s$ cycles. The map $(\sigma,j)\mapsto(j\ n)\sigma$ is a bijection from these pairs onto the permutations $\tau\in S_n$ with $\tau(n)\ne n$ and $n-s$ cycles, with inverse $\tau\mapsto((\tau(n)\ n)\tau,\tau(n))$, and multiplying by $(j\ n)$ inserts $n$ into the cycle of $j$ without changing the cycle count. The two terms therefore exhaust, each element once, the permutations of $S_n$ with exactly $n-s$ cycles. This is the elementary induction behind Garsia's Theorem 5.10 and needs no character theory.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 51-52, and section 3, printed pp. 18-25

items.title: The Gelfand-Tsetlin algebra is the diagonal algebra of the Young basis
items.statement: For $m\ge1$ and $\lambda\vdash m$ let $e^{(m)}_\lambda\in Z(\mathbb C[S_m])$ be the central idempotent of the Wedderburn factor $\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb C})$ of $\mathbb C[S_m]$, so that $1=\sum_{\lambda\vdash m}e^{(m)}_\lambda$ with pairwise orthogonal central idempotents and $e^{(m)}_\lambda$ acts as the identity on $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$ and as $0$ on $S^\mu_{\mathbb C}$ for $\mu\ne\lambda$. For a path $T=(\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(n)})$ in the Young graph (a standard tableau of size $n$) put $P_T:=e^{(1)}_{\lambda^{(1)}}e^{(2)}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\cdots e^{(n)}_{\lambda^{(n)}}$, the factors commuting pairwise. Then: (i) every $P_T$ is a nonzero idempotent of rank one; (ii) $P_TP_{T'}=0$ for $T\ne T'$ and $\sum_T P_T=1$; (iii) $\mathrm{GZ}(n)=\bigoplus_T\mathbb C\,P_T$, the algebra diagonal in the basis of the lines $\mathbb C v_T:=\operatorname{im}P_T$ (the Young basis); (iv) the elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ act diagonally in the Young basis, and $\mathrm{GZ}(n)$ is a maximal commutative subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$.
items.strategy: The complex group algebra is a product of matrix algebras indexed by the Specht modules, so the $e^{(m)}_\lambda$ exist, are orthogonal and sum to $1$. By the multiplicity-free restriction rule, restricted to $S_{m-1}$ the module $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$ is the direct sum of the distinct $S^{\lambda-x}_{\mathbb C}$ over the removable nodes $x$; multiplying by $e^{(m-1)}_{\lambda^{(m-1)}}$ cuts out the single summand of that shape, so by induction on $m$ the partial products $e^{(1)}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\cdots e^{(m)}_{\lambda^{(m)}}$ project onto a one-dimensional space in each irreducible and are rank-one idempotents; orthogonal paths give orthogonal idempotents and the path sum over all shapes is $1$. Each $Z(\mathbb C[S_m])$ lies in this diagonal algebra because a central element of $\mathbb C[S_m]$ acts by the scalar $\omega_{\lambda^{(m)}}$ on the $S_m$-module generated by $v_T$ and by zero on other paths, whence $\mathrm{GZ}(n)$ is contained in, and clearly contains, the span of the $P_T$. An element commuting with all $P_T$ is diagonal in the basis $\{v_T\}$, so the commutant of $\mathrm{GZ}(n)$ is itself and the algebra is maximal commutative; in particular the $X_k$ (which lie in $\mathrm{GZ}(n)$ because $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$ with $T_m\in Z(\mathbb C[S_m])$) act diagonally.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 1-7, printed pp. 7-25
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), sections 3-5, printed pp. 18-45 and Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 51-52

items.statement:
Let $m\ge0$, let $

Then $T_m$ is central in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ and acts on $S^
u_{\mathbb C}$ as the scalar

u=\sum_i inom{

If $m\ge2$, $d_

Count their signs, sum node contents and take traces. No seminormal basis is used.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, Theorem 3.2 and Remark 3.1, printed pp.19-21; coefficient argument reproduced using polytabloids instead of seminormal units
Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Definitions 3.8/3.12 and Theorem 4.4, printed pp.12-16

items.title: The joint spectrum of the Jucys-Murphy elements is the set of tableau content vectors
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$. (a) The elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ act diagonally in the Young basis of the previous item: for every standard tableau $T$ of size $n$ and every $k$, $X_kv_T=c_T(k)v_T$, and the joint eigenspaces are one-dimensional, indexed by the standard tableaux. (b) A vector $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ occurs as the joint eigenvalue vector of a $v_T$, equivalently $\alpha=\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ for a standard tableau $T$, if and only if: (1) $a_1=0$; (2) for every $q>1$ at least one of $a_q-1,a_q+1$ occurs among $a_1,\dots,a_{q-1}$; (3) if $a_p=a_q$ with $p<q$, then both $a_p-1$ and $a_p+1$ occur among $a_{p+1},\dots,a_{q-1}$. The association $T\mapsto\operatorname{Cont}(T)$ is a bijection from the standard tableaux of size $n$ onto this set.
items.strategy: Use the independently proved transposition class-sum scalar and X_k=T_k-T_{k-1} along the branching chain. Prove the addable-content criterion directly from the final occupied diagonal node, then construct the tableau uniquely from each vector satisfying the three conditions; distinct vectors separate the existing Young lines.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 1-7, printed pp. 7-25
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), sections 3-5, printed pp. 18-45 and Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 51-52

items.title: Primitive tableau idempotents by Jucys-Murphy interpolation
items.statement: Let $T$ be a standard tableau of size $n$, let $\mu$ be the shape of the restriction of $T$ to $[n-1]$, and let $A(\mu)$ be the set of contents of the addable nodes of $\mu$. Set $P_{[1]}:=1$ and define recursively, for $n\ge2$, $$P_T:=P_{T\downarrow[n-1]}\prod_{\substack{c\in A(\mu)\\ c\ne c_T(n)}}\frac{X_n-c}{c_T(n)-c}\in\mathbb C[S_n].$$ Then all displayed denominators are nonzero, $P_T$ is the rank-one idempotent projecting onto the Young line $\mathbb C v_T$, each $P_T$ is a polynomial in $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with rational coefficients, and the $P_T$ over the standard tableaux of size $n$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_TP_T=1$.
items.strategy: Induct on $n$. By the joint-spectrum theorem the lines over the partial tableau $T\downarrow[n-1]$ are indexed by the addable nodes of $\mu$, and on the line belonging to an addable node $x$ the element $X_n$ acts by the content $c(x)$; distinct addable nodes have distinct contents by the preceding lemma, so the Lagrange factors send the $c_T(n)$-line to itself with factor $1$ and annihilate every other line over $\mu$, while $P_{T\downarrow[n-1]}$ annihilates all lines whose restriction has a different shape. Hence the product is exactly the projection onto $\mathbb C v_T$; products for different tableaux are orthogonal because distinct lines are, and the sum over all paths of size $n$ is the identity of the diagonal algebra. The recursion exhibits each $P_T$ as a polynomial in the $X_k$ with rational coefficients, starting from $P_{[1]}=1$. This is the source's Theorem 3.4-3.5 interpolation, with its denominators nonzero for the stated reason.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorems 3.4-3.5, printed pp. 22-24
Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 5-6, printed pp. 17-24

items.title: The relative centralizer is generated by the previous centre and the last Jucys-Murphy element
items.statement: Let $n\ge2$ and let $Z(\mathbb C[S_n],\mathbb C[S_{n-1}])=\{z\in\mathbb C[S_n]:zh=hz\text{ for every }h\in S_{n-1}\}$ be the centralizer of $\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]$ in $\mathbb C[S_n]$. Then $$Z(\mathbb C[S_n],\mathbb C[S_{n-1}])=\langle Z(\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]),X_n\rangle,$$ the subalgebra generated by the centre of $\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]$ and the element $X_n$. Consequently $Z(\mathbb C[S_n])\subseteq\langle Z(\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]),X_n\rangle$, because the centre of $\mathbb C[S_n]$ is contained in the centralizer.
items.strategy: The inclusion $\supseteq$ is immediate: class sums of $S_{n-1}$ and the element $X_n=\sum_{j<n}(j\ n)$ commute with $S_{n-1}$ (conjugation permutes the participating transpositions), so both lie in the centralizer. For the reverse inclusion, identify the centralizer with the algebra of functions on the set $E$ of edges $\mu\to\lambda$ of the Young graph: by the Wedderburn decomposition and the multiplicity-free restriction rule each irreducible $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$ contributes $\operatorname{End}_{S_{n-1}}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb C})=\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)}\mathbb C\,p_x$ with $p_x$ the projection onto the summand $S^{\lambda-x}_{\mathbb C}$, and each element of the centralizer is diagonal in the Young basis with eigenvalues constant on the summand, so its eigenvalue function factors through $E$. Here $E$ is in bijection with pairs $(\lambda,x)$; distinct $\lambda$ over one $\mu$ differ by their addable node, whose content is a distinct integer. A central element $z\in Z(\mathbb C[S_{n-1}])$ acts on the $(\lambda,x)$-summand by the central character $\omega_{\lambda-x}(z)$, and distinct shapes have distinct central characters, so the pullbacks of the central characters separate the fibres over distinct $\mu$; the element $X_n$ acts on the $(\lambda,x)$-summand by the scalar $c(x)$ (the joint-spectrum theorem, since the corresponding Young lines lie in that summand), and the addable nodes of $\mu$ have distinct contents, so $X_n$ separates points within each fibre. A unital subalgebra of the algebra of functions on a finite set that separates points is the whole algebra, so the eigenvalue functions of $\langle Z(\mathbb C[S_{n-1}]),X_n\rangle$ fill $\mathbb C^E$; the eigenvalue map is injective on the centralizer, hence the generated subalgebra is all of the centralizer. The route compares the dimension of the centralizer with the multiplicity-free branching graph, as in Okounkov-Vershik Theorem 2.8, with the one-cycle generation step of their Theorem 2.5 replaced by the separation argument detailed above.

items.title: Young's seminormal form from the Jucys-Murphy eigenlines
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and $T^\lambda$ be the standard row-filled tableau of shape $\lambda$. Fix $0\ne v_0\in L_{T^\lambda}$, where $L_T$ is the Young line of $T$. Let $\sigma_T$ be the unique permutation carrying $T^\lambda$ to $T$, put $\ell(T):=\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_T)$, and define $$v_T:=P_T\sigma_Tv_0.$$ These vectors are nonzero and form a basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$. For $s_i=(i\ i+1)$ and $r=c_T(i+1)-c_T(i)$, the same-row and same-column cases give $s_iv_T=v_T$ and $s_iv_T=-v_T$, respectively. Otherwise $T'=s_iT$ is standard and $|r|>1$. When $\ell(T')=\ell(T)+1$, $$s_iv_T=v_{T'}+r^{-1}v_T,\qquad s_iv_{T'}=(1-r^{-2})v_T-r^{-1}v_{T'}.$$ When $\ell(T')=\ell(T)-1$, the equivalent formulas in the original ordering are $$s_iv_T=(1-r^{-2})v_{T'}+r^{-1}v_T,\qquad s_iv_{T'}=v_T-r^{-1}v_{T'}.$$ In particular the matrices of the Coxeter generators in this basis are rational.
items.strategy: Use local relations to split s_i v into the original line and its nonzero swapped-weight component. Construct reduced admissible chains by decreasing row-reading inversions. The leading-term argument makes v_T=P_T sigma_T v_0 nonzero and independent of reduced word. Projecting to the longer line fixes coefficient 1; s_i^2=1 gives the opposite coefficient 1-r^-2 and diagonal -1/r. Reverse ordering is stated explicitly.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 4-6, printed pp. 15-23
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorems 4.2-4.4, printed pp. 26-32

items.title: The Jucys-Murphy elements generate the Gelfand-Tsetlin algebra
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$. Then $$\mathrm{GZ}(n)=\mathbb C[X_1,\dots,X_n],$$ the unital subalgebra generated by the Jucys-Murphy elements; this algebra is the diagonal algebra in the Young basis and is a maximal commutative subalgebra of $\mathbb C[S_n]$.
items.strategy: Interpolation puts every Young projector in the generated unital subalgebra C[X_1,...,X_n]; the diagonal theorem gives GZ contained there. X_k=T_k-T_(k-1) gives the reverse inclusion. Maximality and reduced finite-dimensionality follow from the diagonal algebra, with no algebraic-independence claim.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, Corollary 2.6 and Proposition 1.1, printed pp. 7-12
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorems 3.4-3.5, printed pp. 22-24

items.title: Young's orthogonal form from the seminormal rescaling
items.statement: Rescale each Young vector of the previous item to a unit vector for the positive-definite invariant inner product on the Specht module induced from the tabloid form, chosen with positive square roots. Then for $T$ with $T'=s_iT$ standard and $i,i+1$ in different rows and columns of $T$, in the phasing of the previous item in which $T'$ is the longer tableau, the matrix of $s_i$ on the ordered basis $(v_T,v_{T'})$ is the orthogonal symmetric matrix $$\begin{pmatrix} r^{-1} & \sqrt{1-r^{-2}}\\ \sqrt{1-r^{-2}} & -r^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad r=c_T(i+1)-c_T(i),$$ while the same-row and same-column cases remain the scalars $+1$ and $-1$. In particular each $s_i$ acts by a real orthogonal (hence unitary) involution on each complex Specht module with respect to this inner product, and the resulting matrices form Young's orthogonal representation of $S_n$.
items.strategy: Distinct real joint weights of the self-adjoint X_k make Young lines orthogonal. In the unit basis D=diag(1/norm(v_T),1/norm(v_T′)) gives B=D^-1 A D. Self-adjointness and positive norm ratio make the off-diagonal entries equal and positive; B^2=1 gives sqrt(1-r^-2). The matrices are those of the actual group action.

references.title: Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, section 6, printed pp. 22-24

items.title: Symmetric polynomials in the Jucys-Murphy elements give exactly the centre
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$ and let $f\in\mathbb C[y_1,\dots,y_n]$ be a symmetric polynomial. Then (i) $f(X_1,\dots,X_n)\in Z(\mathbb C[S_n])$; and (ii) conversely, for every central element $z\in Z(\mathbb C[S_n])$ there is a symmetric polynomial $f$ with $z=f(X_1,\dots,X_n)$. In other words, the symmetric polynomial evaluations of the Jucys-Murphy elements are exactly the central elements of the symmetric group algebra.
items.strategy: Symmetry makes the scalar constant on each irreducible shape. Newton identities and content-multiset reconstruction separate the first n power-sum vectors. For each ordered pair of shapes choose the least separating coordinate and multiply only those nonzero-denominator factors. Interpolate all central characters, substitute power sums and use faithfulness.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorem 5.1 with the converse discussion, printed pp. 32-36 and 51-52

title: Jucys–Murphy Elements and Seminormal Forms — Examples

items.title: Elementary Jucys-Murphy class sums through S_4
items.statement: In $S_4$ with $X_2=(1\ 2)$, $X_3=(1\ 3)+(2\ 3)$, $X_4=(1\ 4)+(2\ 4)+(3\ 4)$: the element $e_1(X_2,X_3,X_4)=X_2+X_3+X_4$ is the sum of the six transpositions, the permutations of $S_4$ with $3$ cycles; the element $e_2(X_2,X_3,X_4)$ is the sum of the $11$ permutations with $2$ cycles (the three double transpositions and the eight $3$-cycles); and $e_3(X_2,X_3,X_4)$ is the sum of the six $4$-cycles, the permutations with one cycle. The evaluations are central: $e_1$ and $e_3$ are single class sums, while $e_2$ is the sum of the class sums of types $(2,2)$ and $(3,1)$.
items.strategy: Expand e_1,e_2,e_3 as group-basis sums with 6,11,6 terms. The middle evaluation combines the (3,1) and (2,2) class sums. There are four nonidentity conjugacy classes.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), section 3 and Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 18-25 and 51-52
Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, section 3, printed pp. 12-16

items.title: Ordinary Jucys-Murphy projection formulas do not survive content collision
items.statement: For every field $F$ and every standard tableau $T$ of size $n$, the characteristic-zero interpolation formula $$P_T=P_{T\downarrow[n-1]}\prod_{\substack{c\in A(\mu)\\ c\ne c_T(n)}}\frac{X_n-c}{c_T(n)-c}$$ defines an element of $F[S_n]$ and yields the primitive tableau idempotents of the group algebra over $F$, by the same recursion as over $\mathbb C$.
items.strategy: At the common size-one prefix (1), addable contents 1,-1 collide in F_2 and the first denominator 2 vanishes. The two-dimensional polytabloid module still exists; the calculation refutes only the displayed formula, not existence of other idempotents or a necessary form of modular replacement.

references.title: Andrew Mathas, Seminormal Forms and Gram Determinants for Cellular Algebras, J. reine angew. Math. 619 (2008) 141-173; arXiv:math/0604108, sections 2.8-2.15 and 4 (residues and content collisions in the seminormal/Carter setting), printed pp. 4-8 and 14-21
Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorems 3.4-3.5, printed pp. 22-24

items.title: The Jucys-Murphy spectrum and projectors for S_3
items.statement: The four standard tableaux of size three have content vectors $\operatorname{Cont}=(0,1,2)$ for the row tableau of shape $(3)$, $(0,1,-1)$ for the tableau $\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ of shape $(2,1)$, $(0,-1,1)$ for $\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$, and $(0,-1,-2)$ for the column tableau of shape $(1,1,1)$. Writing $X_2=(1\ 2)$ and $X_3=(1\ 3)+(2\ 3)$ in $\mathbb C[S_3]$, the recursion of [[thm-primitive-tableau-idempotents-by-jucys-murphy-interpolation]] gives the four primitive idempotents $$P_{\mathrm{row}}=\frac{(X_2+1)(X_3+1)}{6},\quad P_{\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}}=\frac{(X_2+1)(2-X_3)}{6},\quad P_{\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}}=\frac{(1-X_2)(X_3+2)}{6},\quad P_{\mathrm{col}}=\frac{(1-X_2)(1-X_3)}{6},$$ with denominators $2$ and $6$; they satisfy $P_T^2=P_T$, $P_TP_{T'}=0$ for $T\ne T'$ and $\sum_TP_T=1$, each $P_T$ acts on its own content vector by the identity and on the other content vectors by zero, and the sum of the two $(2,1)$-projectors is the central idempotent of the two-dimensional Specht module.
items.strategy: Read contents and use stage denominators +/-2 and +/-3, with product 6. Expand all four projectors, verify squares and cross-products, cancel nonidentity coefficients and add 1/6+1/3+1/3+1/6=1. Sum the two middle projectors to get the central shape-(2,1) idempotent.

references.title: Garsia, Young Seminormal Representation, Murphy Elements and Content Evaluations, UCSD lecture notes (2003), Theorems 3.4-3.5, printed pp. 22-24
Okounkov-Vershik, A New Approach to the Representation Theory of the Symmetric Groups, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 2 (1996) 581-605; complete arXiv repost math/0503040, sections 5-6, printed pp. 17-24

items.title: The seminormal and orthogonal blocks for shape (2,1)
items.statement: Let $T=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ and $T'=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ be the two standard tableaux of shape $(2,1)$, so that $s_2T=T'$ and $r:=c_T(3)-c_T(2)=1-(-1)=2$. In the seminormal normalization of the cited theorem the two relations are $$s_2v_{T'}=v_T-\tfrac12v_{T'},\qquad s_2v_T=\tfrac12v_T+\tfrac34v_{T'},$$ so the matrix of $s_2$ in the ordered basis $(v_T,v_{T'})$ with columns the images is $\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1\\3/4&-1/2\end{pmatrix}$; its transpose $\begin{pmatrix}1/2&3/4\\1&-1/2\end{pmatrix}$ records the same images as rows rather than columns. Taking $v_{T'}$ to have unit norm, the longer vector $v_T$ has norm $\sqrt{1-r^{-2}}=\sqrt3/2$, so unit normalization multiplies $v_T$ by $1/\sqrt{1-r^{-2}}=2/\sqrt3$, and the orthogonal form of $s_2$ becomes the symmetric orthogonal block $\begin{pmatrix}1/2&\sqrt3/2\\ \sqrt3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}$. For $s_1$ the entries $1,2$ lie in the same row of $T'$ and in the same column of $T$, so $s_1v_{T'}=+v_{T'}$ and $s_1v_T=-v_T$. Both matrices square to the identity and satisfy $s_1s_2s_1=s_2s_1s_2$ on the two-dimensional Specht module.
items.strategy: The row-filled T′ is shorter and T is longer. Apply the axial-distance -2 formulas in (T′,T), then record columns in (T,T′). Check M^2=I and DMD=MDM. Normalize by E=diag(2/sqrt(3),1); E^-1 M E has positive off-diagonals sqrt(3)/2. Prefix shapes are (1,1) and (2).
